# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXXIV. A Regent’s Girl

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

At Grey Shutters, the subsequent three weeks were filled with activity, as Nell prepared for her departure to Regent’s, requiring a great deal of needlework alongside numerous matters to discuss and organize. Because Obed ensured it, Nell possessed a generous and attractive wardrobe, with Thirza surprisingly raising not a single complaint about any of his purchases or ideas. Furthermore, carrying a bundle of fine, light green fabric in her arms, she walked up to the east gable one night.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0000 }

“Nell, I have a piece of fabric for a lovely light gown for you. It’s likely not an absolute necessity; you possess a great deal of attractive waists; yet it occurred to me that perhaps you would desire something truly elegant to put on should anyone invite you out somewhere during a night in town, for a gathering or an occasion of that nature. It has reached my ears that Odette, Opal, and Flossie possess ‘evening dresses,’ using their terminology, and I have no intention of letting you fall behind them. Mrs. Wace assisted me in selecting it in town during the previous week, and our plan is to have Emily Pettigrew craft it for you. Emily possesses taste, and nobody can match her fits.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0001 }

“Oh, Thirza, this is simply wonderful,” Nell expressed. “I appreciate it very much. You really shouldn't treat me with such goodness—it renders my departure more difficult with each passing day.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0002 }

The green gown was fashioned with all the tucks, frills, and shirrings that Emily’s preference allowed. One night, Nell donned it to show Obed and Thirza, and she performed “The Maiden’s Vow” for their entertainment in the kitchen. Observing the luminous, lively visage and elegant movements, Thirza found her mind drifting to the night Nell had come to Grey Shutters, with recollection bringing forth a clear image of the peculiar, terrified young girl in her absurd yellowish-brown wincey frock, intense sorrow gazing from her eyes full of tears. A element within that remembrance caused tears to spring to Thirza’s eyes as well.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0003 }

“Upon my word, the story I told has brought tears to your eyes, Thirza,” Nell remarked cheerfully, bending down to the chair where Thirza sat to plant a fleeting kiss upon the woman's cheek. “Indeed, I consider that a clear victory.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0004 }

“No, your poem didn’t make me cry,” Thirza declared, as she would have felt humiliated to let mere poetic verse cause her to show such vulnerability. “It’s just that I was unable to stop picturing how you used to be as a small child, Nell. And I found myself hoping you might remain a child forever, despite every one of your strange habits. At this point you are an adult and leaving us; furthermore, wearing that attire makes you appear remarkably tall, elegant, and—and—completely changed—as though Brierley isn't your home anymore—and pondering every bit of it simply made me feel lonely.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0005 }

“Thirza!” Nell positioned herself on Thirza’s gingham-covered lap, held Thirza’s wrinkled face with both hands, and gazed with seriousness and affection into Thirza’s eyes. “I am not altered at all—not in truth. I have merely been trimmed back and grown new limbs. The genuine me—deep inside—remains unaltered. No matter where my journey leads or how extensive my exterior transformations are, it will not alter a single thing; fundamentally, I will perpetually remain your little Nell, loving you, Obed, and beloved Grey Shutters increasingly with each passing day.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0006 }

Nell pressed her youthful, smooth cheek to the withered one belonging to Thirza, extending her hand simultaneously to tap Obed’s shoulder. Thirza longed greatly at that moment to hold the ability Nell had to express her emotions verbally; yet her disposition and custom had decreed a different reality, leaving her capable only of wrapping her arms tightly around her girl and clutching her lovingly to her chest, hoping she would never have to release her.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0007 }

With a suspicious wetness showing in his eyes, Obed stood up and stepped outside. He paced in a state of agitation beneath the stars of the blue summer night, crossing the yard to reach the gate situated under the poplars.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0008 }

“Well now, I suppose she hasn’t been spoiled very much,” he murmured, with pride. “I suppose my stepping in now and then didn’t do much damage when all is said and done. She’s clever and beautiful, and affectionate, too, which surpasses everything else. She’s been a godsend to us, and a more fortunate error than the one Mrs. Tranter made never existed—if luck had anything to do with it. I don’t think it was anything of the sort. It was Divine Intervention, since I calculate the Almighty perceived that we required her.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0009 }

The arrival of the day when Nell had to depart for town lastly occurred. On a splendid September morning, she and Obed journeyed there by carriage, following a tear-filled goodbye with Isolde and a tearless, sensible one—from Thirza's perspective, at any rate—with Thirza. However, once Nell had departed, Isolde wiped her eyes and attended an outing on the shore at Pale Sands alongside a few of her relatives from Delford, where she managed to have a fairly pleasant time; whereas Thirza threw herself violently into unneeded chores and persisted in them the entire day with the most resentful sort of grief—a pain that seethes and consumes and is unable to cleanse itself through easy weeping. Yet during that evening, as Thirza retired to rest, intensely and sorrowfully aware that the small gabled bedchamber at the hallway's termination held no vibrant youthful presence and was untouched by any gentle breath, she pressed her face into her pillow, crying for her child with a fury of weeping that terrified her once she became peaceful enough to ponder the great wickedness of grieving so intensely over a flawed human being.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0010 }

Nell, alongside the remaining scholars from Brierley, arrived in town barely soon enough to rush to the Academy. A flurry of excitement characterized that initial day, which went by agreeably as they met every new student, learned to recognize the professors by sight, and were grouped and arranged into classes. Having been recommended to do so by Miss Thorne, Nell planned to pursue the Second Year work; Hugh Carrow chose to follow the same path. Should they succeed, this choice involved acquiring a First Class teacher’s license within a single year rather than two; nevertheless, it likewise demanded a great deal more labor of a more difficult nature. Because they were unbothered by ambitious impulses, Odette, Opal, Flossie, Wilfred, and Elias Purdy were satisfied to begin the Second Class work. Nell felt a sudden sting of isolation upon realizing she shared a room with fifty different students, every one of them a stranger except for the tall, brown-haired boy on the other side of the space; furthermore, as she morosely considered, her particular acquaintance with him offered little comfort. Even so, she was indisputably pleased regarding their placement in the identical class; their accustomed competition might still continue, and Nell would scarcely have understood how to proceed without its presence.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0011 }

“It would be uncomfortable for me to be without it,” was her thought. “Hugh appears remarkably resolute. Right now, in this place, I imagine he is deciding to capture the medal. His chin is so magnificent! It never caught my attention until now. If only Odette and Opal had also entered for First Class. Even so, once I become familiar with everyone, I probably will not feel quite so out of place. I am curious about which girls in this room will become my friends. Contemplating it is truly fascinating. Naturally, I gave my word to Isolde that I would never hold any Regent’s girl as close to my heart as I hold her, regardless of how much I affection I develop for her; nevertheless, I possess plenty of secondary affection to share. That girl who has brown eyes and a crimson waist appeals to me. Vibrant and rosy-red is how she appears; then there is the pale, light-haired one who is staring through the window. Her hair is exquisite, and she has the appearance of someone who understands a bit about dreams. Getting to know both of them would be wonderful for me—knowing them thoroughly—enough to wrap my arm around their waists as we walk, and to use pet names for them. However, at this precise moment, we are strangers to one another, and they likely have no special desire to get to know me. Oh, how lonely it is!”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0012 }

A deeper solitude settled over Nell as dusk fell and she remained by herself in her hall bedroom that evening. Because every other girl had local kin to show her compassion, Nell was not going to live with them. Although Miss Lavinia Pembroke desired to host her, the great distance between Beechwood and the Academy made this impossible; consequently, Miss Pembroke searched for a rooming house, guaranteeing to Obed and Thirza that Nell would find it ideal.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0013 }

“The woman managing it is a lady of diminished fortune,” Miss Pembroke clarified. “A British officer was her husband, and she exercises great caution regarding the kind of boarders she accepts. Under her roof, Nell will never encounter any undesirable people. Good food is served, and the residence stands close to the Academy, situated within a peaceful area.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0014 }

Though all of this could be entirely correct, as it ultimately turned out to be, it brought no real comfort to Nell when she was overcome by the initial pangs of homesickness. She gazed despondently around the small, cramped bedchamber, taking in its unadorned, drab-papered walls, its tiny iron bedframe, and its vacant bookshelf; meanwhile, a terrible lump formed in her throat at the memory of her white bedroom at Grey Shutters, where she could comfortably feel the presence of the expansive, quiet green outdoors, the sweet peas blooming in the garden, the moonlight shining over the orchard, the stream running down the slope, the spruce branches swaying in the evening breeze further off, the immense starry heavens, and the glow from Isolde’s window beaming through the opening among the trees. Nothing like that existed in this place; Nell was aware that just beyond her window lay a paved street, a web of telephone wires blocking the sky, the footsteps of unfamiliar passersby, and countless lights illuminating the faces of strangers. Realizing that tears were imminent, she tried to resist them.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0015 }

“I will not weep. It is foolish—and feeble—a third tear has dropped past my nose. Further ones are arriving! I need to recall something amusing to prevent them. Yet nothing is amusing unless it relates to Brierley, and that merely aggravates matters—four—five—I am returning home on the coming Friday, though that feels a century off. Oh, Obed has almost reached home by this time—and Thirza stands at the gate, gazing along the lane to spot him—six—seven—eight—oh, counting them is pointless! They will be pouring out like a deluge shortly. I am unable to feel happier—I have no desire to feel happier. Being wretched is preferable!”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0016 }

A torrent of weeping undoubtedly would have arrived if Flossie Tulk had not shown up right then. Because she was happy to behold an acquainted visage, Nell no longer remembered that she and Flossie had never shared much affection. Even a Tulk was a sight she received gladly as a piece of Brierley existence.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0017 }

“I’m really happy you made the trip up,” Nell remarked with genuine warmth.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0018 }

“You’ve been weeping,” Flossie observed, showing an irritating sympathy. “I imagine you’re missing home—certain folks possess so little restraint regarding that. I certainly don't plan to be homesick, let me assure you. City life is far too wonderful after that dull old Brierley. I marvel at how I managed to survive there for such a long time. You ought not to weep, Nell; it fails to flatter you, because your nose and eyes turn crimson, making you appear completely flushed. I had an absolutely delightful experience at the Academy today. Our French instructor is a total sweetheart. The sight of his moustache would make your heart flutter. Do you possess any food nearby, Nell? I am genuinely ravenous. Ah, I suspected it was probable Thirza would pack you full of cake. That is the reason I came by. If not for that, I would have proceeded to the park so I could listen to the band perform alongside Frank Stockley. He resides at the same lodging as I do, and he is a fun-loving fellow. He spotted you during class today, and inquired of me who the auburn-haired girl was. I informed him that you were an orphan whom the Abernethys had taken in, and no one understood a great deal regarding what your background was prior to that.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0019 }

Nell was questioning whether being alone and weeping might actually be preferable to Flossie Tulk’s company when Odette and Opal arrived, both boastfully wearing an inch of Regent’s color ribbon—scarlet and purple—pinned upon their coats. Because Flossie was not “speaking” to Odette at that moment, she was forced to settle into a state of relative harmlessness.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0020 }

“Well,” Odette uttered with a sigh, “it seems to me like I’ve existed through numerous moons since this morning. My presence is required at home to review my Virgil—twenty lines were assigned to us by that miserable old professor to begin tomorrow. Tonight, however, settling down to study was simply impossible for me. Nell, it appears to me that I spot evidence of weeping. Own up if you have been crying. My self-respect will be restored by it, since I was crying abundantly until Opal arrived. Being a goose does not bother me quite as much when another person is also goosey. Cake? A teeny slice will be given to me by you, won't it? Thank you. The genuine Brierley flavor is present in it.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0021 }

Noticing the Regent’s calendar resting on the table, Opal inquired whether Nell intended to compete for the gold medal.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0022 }

Her face reddened as Nell acknowledged that the thought had crossed her mind.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0023 }

“Oh, I almost forgot,” Flossie remarked, “Regent’s will receive a scholarship from Avery in the end. Information arrived today. I learned it from Frank Stockley—you are aware that his uncle serves on the board of governors. Tomorrow, the Academy will announce it.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0024 }

A scholarship for Avery! Nell was conscious of her heart thumping faster, and as though through enchantment, the boundaries of her hope moved and expanded. Prior to Flossie sharing the information, the absolute summit of Nell's desires had been a provincial license for teaching, First Class, when the year concluded, and maybe the medal! Yet presently, within a single instant, Nell envisioned herself gaining the Avery scholarship, pursuing an Arts degree at Wexcombe College, and finishing her studies wearing a gown and mortar board, even before the reverberation of Flossie’s statement had faded. Because the Avery scholarship was awarded in English, and Nell believed that in this subject she stood upon familiar ground.
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0025 }

A rich maker of goods from New Brunswick passed away, bequeathing a portion of his wealth to fund numerous scholarships that were to be divided among different academies and high schools in the Maritime Provinces, based on their individual ranks. Considerable uncertainty had existed regarding whether Regent’s would receive one, yet the issue was finally resolved, and when the year concluded, two hundred and fifty dollars annually for four years at Wexcombe College would be awarded to the graduate achieving the top score in English and English Literature. It was no surprise that Nell’s cheeks were burning as she retired to bed that evening!
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0026 }

“I will secure that scholarship if I can achieve it through hard work,” she determined. “Wouldn’t Obed feel pride if I managed to become a B.A.? Oh, having ambitions brings such delight. I am extremely pleased that I possess so many. And the finest part is that they never appear to cease. The moment you reach one goal, you spot another sparkling even higher above. It renders existence so captivating.”
{: #nw-v01-c34-p0027 }
